items.signText: PAPER AND CARD ONLY. Please flatten all boxes before you put them in. Pizza boxes with food on them cannot be recycled and should go in the black bin instead.
items.question: What does the sign tell people?
options: a) Food waste may be put in this bin with the card.
b) All cardboard boxes should be thrown in the black bin.
c) Pizza boxes that are dirty must not go in this bin.
items.explanation: The sign says "Pizza boxes with food on them cannot be recycled and should go in the black bin instead", so dirty pizza boxes must not go in the paper bin. The bin is for "PAPER AND CARD ONLY", so food is not allowed, and clean boxes go in this bin once they are flattened, not in the black bin.

items.signText: Volunteers meet outside the library at 10 am. Children under 12 are welcome but must come with an adult. There’s a free lunch for everyone who helps! Please sign up online by Thursday so that we can order enough food.
items.question: Why should people sign up before Thursday?
options: a) So that each child can be given an adult to work with
b) So that the organisers know how much lunch to get
c) Because only a small number of volunteers can join
items.explanation: The notice asks people to sign up "by Thursday so that we can order enough food" for the "free lunch". Nothing limits the number of volunteers, and children "must come with an adult" – the organisers do not find one for them.

items.signText: Glass bottles and jars go in the green containers. Please remove the lids first. From 1 March, we can no longer accept window glass or mirrors – please take these to the general waste area next to the car park.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) Mirrors must be taken to another area.
b) Bottles and jars must be washed before you recycle them.
c) Window glass should go in the green containers.
items.explanation: The notice says the centre can "no longer accept window glass or mirrors" and asks people to "take these to the general waste area", so mirrors go somewhere else. Window glass is exactly what the green containers no longer take, and the notice asks people to remove lids, not to wash bottles.

items.signText: Because of the bank holiday on Monday, all bin collections next week will be one day later than usual. Garden waste will not be collected at all next week. Normal collections start again the week after.
items.question: What is the email about?
options: a) Residents should put their bins out on Monday morning.
b) Garden waste will no longer be collected after this week.
c) Next week, bins will be collected a day late.
items.explanation: The email says "all bin collections next week will be one day later than usual" because of the bank holiday. Garden waste stops only for one week, as "Normal collections start again the week after", and Monday is mentioned only as the bank holiday, not as a collection day.

items.signText: Hi Tom, the beach clean-up on Saturday starts at 9, not 10 as it says on the poster. Gloves and rubbish bags are provided, but bring your own water – there’s no café nearby. See you there! Priya
items.question: Why has Priya written to Tom?
options: a) To suggest meeting at a café before they start
b) To give him the correct start time
c) To ask him to bring bags for everyone
items.explanation: Priya writes that the clean-up "starts at 9, not 10 as it says on the poster", so she is correcting the time Tom has seen. Bags are already "provided", so Tom does not need to bring them, and she says "there’s no café nearby", so she is not suggesting meeting at one.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: The teenager who fixes the city’s bikes
lesenParts.text:
Josh Turner was nineteen when he opened his bicycle repair shop in Leeds. Three years later, the little shop near the canal is busy every day. However, the beginning was not easy.

Josh has loved bikes all his life. His grandfather taught him to mend punctures in the garden shed. “I spent every weekend with oily hands,” he says. At school he was not interested in most subjects, because he preferred taking things apart and putting them back together. After school he started an engineering course at college, but he left after one year. “The course was mostly theory. I wanted to work with real machines,” he explains.

For the next year he repaired bikes for friends and neighbours in his parents’ garage. He charged very little, so soon strangers were knocking on the door with broken bikes. His parents were patient, but the garage was always full. In the end, his mother told him to find a proper workplace.

Josh found an empty shop with a cheap rent, but the problem was money. The banks did not want to lend money to a teenager with no business experience. Finally, his uncle lent him £4,000 for tools and spare parts. Josh promised to pay it all back within two years. He managed it in eighteen months.

The first winter was hard because few people cycle in cold, wet weather, and customers were rare. Some weeks Josh earned almost nothing. He used the quiet time well, though, and built a simple website and started posting short repair videos. In them he shows easy jobs, like adjusting gears or cleaning a chain. Some customers were surprised. “Why do you teach people to fix their own bikes? You’ll lose business!” they said. Josh disagrees. “People watch the videos and try the job at home. Sometimes something goes really wrong. Then they remember my name. They trust me, because I’ve already helped them for free.”

Today Josh employs two part-time mechanics, both students. He also runs a free repair class for local children every Saturday morning. “Lots of kids have bikes with flat tyres in the garage. Nobody shows them how to fix them,” he says.

What advice would he give to other young people? “Don’t wait until you know everything. I made plenty of mistakes in my first year. I ordered the wrong parts, and I forgot to keep receipts. But every mistake taught me something useful.” He smiles. “And find an uncle with some savings!”

questions.question: Why did Josh leave his college course?
questions.explanation: Josh says: "The course was mostly theory. I wanted to work with real machines." He wanted practical work. The text never says the course was too difficult, and he opened the shop only later, after a year of repairs in the garage.
options: a) He had already opened his own shop.
b) He found the work far too difficult.
c) He wanted to do more practical work.
d) He needed to earn money for his family.

questions.question: Why did Josh stop working in his parents’ garage?
questions.explanation: The text says: "In the end, his mother told him to find a proper workplace." The neighbours were his customers, not people who complained, and nothing is said about the university or customers getting lost.
options: a) He wanted to be closer to the university.
b) His mother asked him to find somewhere else.
c) His customers could not find the house.
d) The neighbours complained about the noise.

questions.question: What do we learn about the money Josh borrowed?
questions.explanation: Josh "promised to pay it all back within two years. He managed it in eighteen months", so he paid it back early. The banks "did not want to lend money" to him, and the money was "for tools and spare parts", not for the rent.
options: a) He paid it back sooner than he had promised.
b) A bank lent it to him after several attempts.
c) His uncle later let him keep it as a gift.
d) He spent most of it on the rent for the shop.

questions.question: What does Josh think about his online repair videos?
questions.explanation: Josh explains that when "something goes really wrong", viewers "remember my name. They trust me", so the videos bring him customers. Some customers fear he will "lose business", but Josh disagrees with them.
options: a) They bring him customers in the end.
b) They take up too much of his free time.
c) They were a mistake in his first winter.
d) They have reduced the number of repairs he gets.

questions.question: What is the main advice Josh gives to other young people?
questions.explanation: Josh says: "Don’t wait until you know everything" and "every mistake taught me something useful." Forgetting receipts is only one example of his mistakes, not his main advice, and planning every detail is the opposite of what he says.
options: a) Keep a careful record of everything you buy.
b) Plan every detail before you start.
c) Find a partner with business experience.
d) Start now and learn from your mistakes.

lesenParts.textTitle: Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit
lesenParts.text:
Last spring, my partner and I adopted a three-year-old dog called Biscuit from a rescue centre near Leeds. The staff told us that he had spent most of his life alone in a small back garden. (1) ________ For the first two days, he hid behind the sofa and refused to eat anything at all.

In the end, we contacted a local trainer called Megan Hughes. On her first visit, she did not bring any equipment with her. (2) ________ For an hour, she simply sat on the floor with a book and completely ignored Biscuit. By the end of that hour, he was lying next to her feet.

Megan explained that many rescue dogs need time before they can learn anything. (3) ________ So we kept the same routine every day: a walk at seven, breakfast at eight and a quiet hour in the afternoon. After about three weeks, Biscuit started to relax.

Then the real training began. We used tiny pieces of cheese as rewards, and the lessons never lasted more than five minutes. (4) ________ Biscuit learned to sit in a single afternoon, but learning to stay took him much longer.

The hardest part was the park. Other dogs frightened him, and he barked at every bicycle. (5) ________ Now, a year later, he can walk past a busy playground without even looking up. He still hides behind the sofa sometimes, but these days it is usually because he has stolen a sock.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 1?
questions.explanation: Biscuit had lived "alone in a small back garden", so a busy flat full of noise and visitors would be a shock; this explains why next "he hid behind the sofa". The sentence about him loving other dogs from the first day cannot fit, because it does not match a dog that hides and refuses to eat.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 2?
questions.explanation: "This surprised us" refers back to "she did not bring any equipment", and the writers expected "a whistle or at least a lead". The sentence saying she arrived with a bag of toys and a lead is wrong, because the text says she brought no equipment.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 3?
questions.explanation: "Before that" means before dogs "can learn anything", and "a regular routine helps" leads directly to "So we kept the same routine every day". No other sentence explains why the writers started a routine.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.explanation: The lessons "never lasted more than five minutes", and this sentence gives the reason: "short, happy lessons work much better than long ones". The sentence saying cheese was the only food he would not eat is wrong, because the writers "used tiny pieces of cheese as rewards".
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 5?
questions.explanation: "there" refers to "the park", and an "almost empty" park solves the problem that "Other dogs frightened him". The sentence saying he loved meeting other dogs contradicts "Other dogs frightened him".
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text: When I started college last year, a friend persuaded me to join the student radio station. I had never (1) ______ on the radio before, so I was extremely nervous at my first meeting. Luckily, the station manager, Priya, was very kind. She (2) ______ me to start by reading the weather report, which only (3) ______ about two minutes. Even so, my hands were shaking the first time the red light came on. Little by little, it got easier. After a couple of months I felt (4) ______ enough to ask for my own music programme, and Priya agreed. Now, every Thursday evening from eight to nine, I (5) ______ songs by new bands from our area and chat about them with guests. Some listeners even send messages to request their favourite tracks. Working at the station has (6) ______ me how to plan my time and how to work as part of a team. Next term I am hoping to interview a few local musicians live in the studio, which will be my biggest challenge so far.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: The text says "I had never spoken on the radio before". Speak can be used without an object; told, said and explained all need an object (told someone, said something, explained something), so they cannot fit here.
options: a) said
b) spoken
c) explained
d) told

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: Only advise follows the pattern verb + person + to-infinitive: "She advised me to start by reading the weather report". We cannot say suggested me to, insisted me to or proposed me to.
options: a) proposed
b) suggested
c) advised
d) insisted

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: The weather report "only lasted about two minutes": last means continue for a period of time. Spent needs a person as subject (I spent two minutes), passed needs time as subject, and kept does not describe how long something takes.
options: a) passed
b) kept
c) lasted
d) spent

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: At first the writer was "extremely nervous", but "after a couple of months" felt confident enough to ask for a programme. Being polite, careful or patient enough does not explain why the writer could now ask to present a show.
options: a) confident
b) polite
c) careful
d) patient

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: A radio presenter plays songs: "I play songs by new bands from our area". Put songs and turn songs are not correct English, and make songs would mean the writer writes the music.
options: a) put
b) turn
c) make
d) play

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: The structure is "has taught me how to plan my time": teach + person + how to. Learnt, studied and practised cannot be followed by a person (me) in this way.
options: a) learnt
b) studied
c) practised
d) taught

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text: Last autumn our town council asked local people to help plant five hundred young trees along the river path. The project had (1) ______ planned for over a year, but the money only arrived in the summer. On a cold Saturday morning about sixty volunteers met at the old bridge, carrying spades and flasks of hot tea. Very (2) ______ of us had ever planted a tree before, so a gardener from the council showed us what to do. By lunchtime my back was aching, and the work was far (3) ______ tiring than I had expected. Still, it felt good to see the long line of thin trees standing in the grass. The gardener explained that the trees are too young to look after (4) ______ yet. They will not survive their first summer (5) ______ someone waters them regularly. The council has now organised a rota, (6) ______ means that every volunteer spends one evening a month with a watering can. My turn is next Tuesday, and I am already looking forward to it.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: This is a past perfect passive: "The project had been planned for over a year". The project did not plan anything itself, so had must be followed by been + past participle.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: "Very few of us had ever planted a tree before, so a gardener … showed us what to do." The word so shows that most people had no experience; very many would not fit the meaning or the word ever.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: Tiring is a long adjective, so the comparative is more tiring than. "My back was aching" shows that the work was harder than expected, so less is not possible.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The subject is the trees, so the reflexive pronoun is needed: "the trees are too young to look after themselves yet". Them would mean some other things, not the trees.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: Unless means if not: "They will not survive their first summer unless someone waters them regularly". If would give the opposite meaning (watering would kill them).

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: After a comma, a non-defining relative clause that refers to the whole idea before it starts with which: "organised a rota, which means that every volunteer …". That cannot be used after a comma.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Look, I’ve bought this scarf for my aunt.
Man: It’s lovely. Was it expensive?
Woman: Well, the label said thirty pounds, but there was a sale on, so it was twenty-four. And then the shop assistant noticed a small mark on it and took another six pounds off.
Man: So you paid eighteen pounds? That’s a good price. I can hardly see the mark.

Man: Have you got anything for your brother’s birthday yet? Oliver’s going to be sixteen, isn’t he?
Woman: Yes, and I’ve finally found something. I was going to get him a shirt for his football team, but they didn’t have his size.
Man: What about that board game he keeps talking about?
Woman: Mum’s already bought him that. So in the end I got him some headphones. His old ones are broken.
Man: Good idea. He’ll use them every day.

Man: I’ve decided what to give my mum and dad for their wedding anniversary. I’m taking them out for a meal at that new Italian restaurant.
Woman: How lovely! The anniversary’s on Friday, isn’t it?
Man: Yes, but Dad doesn’t finish work until nine on Fridays. I wanted to go on Saturday evening instead, but the restaurant was fully booked. So we’re going for lunch on Sunday.
Woman: That sounds perfect.

Woman: Good afternoon, shoppers. If you’re looking for that special present, don’t forget our gift-wrapping service on the ground floor. Our normal closing time is half past five, but this week, to help with your Christmas shopping, the store is staying open until seven o’clock. Please note that the gift-wrapping desk closes earlier, at six. Thank you for shopping with us.

Woman: I can’t decide which bag to get for Lucy. This striped one is fun.
Man: Hmm, but she isn’t really a beach person, is she? What about the black backpack? She cycles to work.
Woman: She’s just bought one, actually. No, I think she’d like the brown leather one best. It goes with everything.
Man: It’s more expensive, though.
Woman: That’s fine. She’s my best friend.

Woman: Are you going to Rachel’s leaving party at the office tomorrow?
Man: Yes, and I still haven’t got her anything. I thought about flowers, but they’ll be dead in a week.
Woman: She loves cooking, doesn’t she? What about a recipe book?
Man: She’s got hundreds of those. No, I know. She’s always saying her desk looks empty, so I’ll get her a little plant for her new office.
Woman: Perfect. She’ll love that.

Woman: Granny’s eightieth birthday is next month. What shall we give her?
Man: You’re good at baking. Why don’t you make her a cake?
Woman: Auntie Sue’s already making one. We could make her a birthday card, I suppose.
Man: She’ll get lots of cards. What about putting some old family photos into an album?
Woman: Oh yes, she’d love that. Let’s start looking for photos this weekend.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Nice watch! Is that one of those smart watches?
Man: Yes. Everyone thinks I got it for my messages, but my phone’s fine for that.
Woman: So is it for running?
Man: Not really. The doctor said I wasn’t sleeping enough, so I wanted to know how many hours I really get each night. The watch shows me every morning. It’s already made me go to bed earlier.
Woman: And it looks good too.
Man: That’s just a bonus.

Woman: Are you still using that running app?
Man: Every day! I know it isn’t free, and it took me a few days to understand all the buttons, but now it’s easy. Honestly, without it I’d have stopped running weeks ago. When it tells me I’ve beaten my best time, I just want to go out again the next morning.
Woman: Maybe I should try it, then.
Man: You should. It’s worth every penny.

Man: How are you getting on with the new booking system?
Woman: Not very well! I’m sure it’s better than the old one, but nobody showed us how it works.
Man: Exactly. We had one short email from the manager and that was it. They should have given us a proper course before it started.
Woman: I agree. I spent half the morning asking people for help.
Man: Me too. Maybe it’ll save us time when we know what we’re doing, but I’m not so sure.

Man: So did your family really spend a whole evening without phones?
Woman: We did. To be honest, I thought I’d hate it. I thought I’d keep worrying about missing messages.
Man: And did you?
Woman: For about ten minutes! Then we got a board game out and laughed all evening. My kids didn’t even ask for their phones. We’re going to do it every Friday now.

Woman: I had my first video call with Grandma and Grandad last night.
Man: How did it go? I bet it took ages to get them connected.
Woman: That’s what I expected! I was ready to spend an hour explaining which buttons to press. But Grandad had practised with a neighbour, and it worked first time. We chatted for ages, and I could hear them perfectly.
Man: That’s brilliant.
Woman: Honestly, it was the best part of my week.

Man: Are you still learning Spanish with that app?
Woman: No, I gave up last month.
Man: Really? I thought it was free.
Woman: It is, and the games were fun. I learned loads of words. But when I went to Valencia, I couldn’t have a single conversation with anyone. All I’d done was press buttons! So now I go to an evening class where we actually talk to each other.
Man: That sounds much more useful.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsley Theatre. My name’s Helen and I’ll be your guide this morning. The tour takes about an hour, so I hope you’re all wearing comfortable shoes.

Let’s start with a bit of history. A lot of visitors think this building was once a church, because of the tall windows, but in fact it was built as a fish market. It only became a theatre in 1904, when a local businessman bought it and turned it into the place you see today.

Now, if you follow me into the main hall… Here we are. When the theatre first opened, it had space for twelve hundred people, but in those days the seats were very narrow. After we put in new, more comfortable seats ten years ago, the number went down, and today we have eight hundred and fifty seats.

Do look up at the ceiling. People usually expect a theatre ceiling to be red, but ours is green, with little gold stars painted all over it. It was cleaned last spring, so the colours are really bright again.

Next we’re going backstage. Down these stairs is the workshop where the costumes are made. We have a team of four people who make everything by hand. The wigs, by the way, aren’t made here. We order those from a company in London.

Right, now we’re on the stage itself. You’re welcome to walk around, and you can even sit on the furniture, which is from tonight’s show. The only thing I must ask is that you don’t touch the ropes at the side of the stage. They hold up the scenery, and they’re very heavy.

That’s nearly the end of the tour. Before you go, keep hold of your ticket. If you show it in the café on the ground floor, you’ll get ten per cent off anything you buy there today. I’m afraid the discount doesn’t work in the gift shop, though. Thank you all for coming, and I hope you enjoy the rest of your day.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking to Megan Price, who opened her own bakery in the town of Ludlow two years ago. Megan, you used to work in an office, didn’t you?

Megan: That’s right, I was in a bank for six years. The pay was fine and my colleagues were lovely, so people were surprised when I left. But I’d been baking at weekends for years, and I realised that Saturday mornings in the kitchen were the only time I felt really happy. In the end, I just couldn’t keep doing a job I didn’t care about.

Interviewer: How did you feel on the day the shop opened?

Megan: Honestly, I was terrified. Not about the baking, because I knew my bread was good. I kept thinking: what if I’ve spent all my savings and nobody comes through the door? Then at half past seven there was a queue outside, and I nearly cried.

Interviewer: Bakers start work very early. How do you cope with that?

Megan: I start at four. Everyone warned me it would be awful, but actually I don’t mind it at all. The streets are quiet, the radio’s on, and I get more done in those two hours than I used to in a whole day at the bank. What I do find hard is going to bed at nine.

Interviewer: What makes a good bakery, in your opinion?

Megan: Lots of people would say the recipes, and of course they matter. But for me, it’s the people behind the counter. If customers feel welcome, if you remember their names and what they like, they’ll come back even on a day when the croissants aren’t perfect.

Interviewer: A lot of people buy their bread in supermarkets. Does that worry you?

Megan: Not really. Some supermarket bread is perfectly nice, and it’s cheaper than mine, I know that. But I don’t think we’re really competing. People come to me for a treat, or for something special at the weekend, not for their everyday sandwich loaf.

Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who’d like to start their own business?

Megan: Don’t wait until everything is perfect, because it never will be. But do get some experience first. I worked in another baker’s shop on Saturdays for a year before I opened mine, and I learned more there than from any book.

Interviewer: Megan Price, thank you very much.

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Sophie and the notes you have made.

From: Sophie
Subject: A job at the café

Hi!
Guess what? The café where I work, Bean There, is looking for someone to help at weekends, and I immediately thought of you! [Note 1: Brilliant!] You’d work on Saturday and Sunday mornings from eight o’clock until one. Would those hours be OK for you? [Note 2: Explain] The work is mainly serving customers and clearing tables, but sometimes you’d help in the kitchen too. Which would you prefer to do? [Note 3: Tell Sophie] If you’re interested, my manager would like to meet you next week. When are you free? [Note 4: Suggest a day and time]

Love,
Sophie

Write your email to Sophie using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 – Article
You see this announcement in an English-language magazine for young people.

Articles wanted!
MY FIRST JOB
What was your first job, or what job would you like to do first? What did you learn, or what would you like to learn? Was it what you expected?
Write an article answering these questions. We will publish the best articles in our magazine.

Write your article.

Question 3 – Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
It was my first day at work and I was late.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 1 – Interview
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question and give some extra information.

Where do you live?
Can you tell us something about your home?
Which room in your home do you like best? Why?
What do you like about your neighbourhood?
Is there anything you would like to change about the area where you live?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 2 – Photo description
Look at the photograph. It shows a family doing jobs together in a kitchen. An adult is washing dishes at the sink, a teenager is drying plates with a towel and a young child is putting knives and forks into a drawer. A dog is sitting on the floor next to the child. The kitchen is bright, and there is a bowl of fruit on the table. Everyone is smiling. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.

Talk for about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 3 – Collaborative task
The local council wants to make a neighbourhood a better place for young people. Here are some ideas they are thinking about.

a skate park
a youth club with games and music
a free outdoor cinema in summer
more cycle paths
a community garden
free sports lessons at weekends

Talk together about how each idea could help young people in the neighbourhood. Then decide which idea would be the best.

Talk together for about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 4 – General conversation
The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about homes and neighbours. Give your opinion and talk to your partner too.

Do you know your neighbours well? Why or why not?
How can neighbours help each other?
Is it better to live in a city or in the countryside? Why?
What do young people in your area do in their free time?
What kind of home would you like to live in in the future?
